steps.title: Just walking
steps.text: This is you, walking down a street, not looking for anything in particular.
quotes: System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary control.

steps.title: Light reaches the eye
steps.text: Light from the billboard passes the cornea and the lens and lands on the retina at the back of the eye, upside down and mirrored.
quotes: It allows light to enter, and along with the lens, focuses light onto the retina.
The visual field projects onto the retina through the lenses and falls on the retinae as an inverted, reversed image.
steps.time: t0: the billboard comes into view

steps.title: Two roads out of the eye
steps.text: At the optic chiasm half the fibres cross, so the right side of what you see goes to the left half of the brain. Most go to the thalamus; a branch goes to the superior colliculus.
quotes: Within each eye, the axons projecting from the medial side of the retina decussate at the optic chiasm.
Another target of the optic tract is the superior colliculus.

steps.title: First stop in the cortex
steps.text: The thalamus passes the signal on to the primary visual cortex, at the back of the brain.
quotes: We find a mean onset latency of activity over occipital cortex (C1(e)) at 56 ms, with dorsolateral frontal cortex subsequently active by just 80 ms.
Visual responses occurred in V1 before any other cortical area.
steps.time: ~56 ms after it comes into view

steps.title: The brightest thing wins
steps.text: Before you decide to look, your brain picks out what stands out most, and your eyes jump to it.
quotes: Models of visual attention postulate the existence of a saliency map whose function is to guide attention and gaze to the most conspicuous regions in a visual scene.
This ventral frontoparietal network works as a 'circuit breaker' for the dorsal system, directing attention to salient events.
steps.time: eyes land: ~100 ms at the fastest, usually later

steps.title: What is it? Edges, angles, a sign
steps.text: Along the underside of the brain, each stage responds to something more complex than the last: short edges in V1, then angles, then whole objects. Around 100 ms after your eyes land, it is already "a sign".
quotes: “core object recognition,” the ability to rapidly recognize objects despite substantial appearance variation, is solved in the brain via a cascade of reflexive, largely feedforward computations that culminate in a powerful neuronal representation in the inferior temporal cortex.
We could decode object category information from human visual cortex in single trials as early as 100 ms poststimulus.
It was proposed that each stage of this hierarchy created successively more complex representations by aggregating the output of the simpler feature detectors in the previous stage

the functional properties of single cells within V2 were well predicted by a simple aggregation of responses across several V1 cells, with a slight increase in both receptive field (RF) size and selectivity for more complex stimuli (angles) than the orientation selectivity observed in V1.
anatomical evidence indicates that the ventral pathway is actually a complex network of feedforward and feedback projections

steps.title: You've read it before deciding to
steps.text: A patch of the left fusiform gyrus knows what written words look like. It even responds to words too brief to see, so a sign gets read without you trying.
quotes: the VWF system was revealed as a strictly left-hemispheric activation which, in control subjects, was identical for stimuli presented in the left or in the right hemifield and was located in the middle portion of the left fusiform gyrus.
High frequency words (180ms) were distinguishable from pseudowords earliest
steps.time: ~180 ms after the eyes land (a common word)

steps.title: It means something to you
steps.text: Studies in monkeys trace connections from here to areas for emotion, memory and value.
quotes: occipitotemporo-ventral striatum pathway, which also originates in aIT and supports the assignment of stimulus valence
brand knowledge for one of the drinks had a dramatic influence on expressed behavioral preferences and on the measured brain responses.

steps.title: A fraction of a second, no effort
steps.text: Light, the eye jump, the object, the word, the meaning: none of it needed a decision from you.
quotes: The control of attention is shared by the two systems.

steps.title: Epilogue: next time, it feels familiar
steps.text: Days later you pass the billboard again. Seeing something again tends to make people like it a little more, up to a point.
quotes: the mere exposure effect was characterized by a positive slope and negative quadratic effect consistent with an inverted-U shaped curve
